The same difficulty applies to the claim that producing the absolute good necessarily follows from God’s essence. That consequence comes after the essence of the whole, so how can it be God’s own causality? If “the whole” means a collection of many essences, there is no single essence of the whole; then there is no single necessary act of producing it, but many necessary acts producing many effects. These cannot be identical with God. — T. M. (editor).

God is all existence, and existence is all His; He is all perfection, and all perfection is His. As the author says in his Sanctifications, His exaltedness and glory do not depend on His being creator or knower at the level where creatures exist. He is Creator without a created thing and Knower without an object of knowledge, because all existence flows from Him and each being is contained in Him in its highest mode. — س قده

As explained earlier, the added feature is not itself an effect. It is the act of producing, like a grammatical relation that is neither subject nor object. In the discussion of cause and effect, the author explicitly says that unrestricted existence is not an effect but God’s true causality. See that discussion. — س قده

One might say this must be the right account, since the two things cannot be at the same level: the feature causes the First Intellect, and cause and effect are not at the same level. The author’s point to the master is that he must either accept a contradiction or accept that many things come from the One. Since the First Intellect is assumed to be the first effect, the causal feature must be at its level, or else there is a contradiction. But if one accepts the contradiction, it does not follow that many effects come from the One; instead, there is an infinite regress, because the later necessary consequence is the effect. Or the regress ends in a feature identical with the essence. — س قده

It would be better to say that this is merely relational causality, which is not at issue. But the author’s claim is also challenged by God’s additional relational attributes, which everyone accepts are pure relations, and even by the concepts of real attributes: as concepts, they are distinct from the essence in thought, though identical with it in reality. — س قده

This is a strange claim. The two respects become one, even though they give rise to one effect. But that is not so: unrestricted, all-embracing existence differs from limited existence; the greatest manifestation differs from what it manifests; the Great Human differs from the spirit of that human—the purely intelligible realm—from the whole of the bodily, angelic, and intelligible realms. Their relation is like that between the simple intellect described in the book on the soul and the Perfect Human. If existence has levels, the First Intellect is one level, while the Great Human is the whole range of created levels. The all-embracing existence is their preserved source, because what distinguishes existences is itself what they share. God’s being the source of unrestricted existence is not the same as His being the source of only the separate intellectual existence; the former is identical with His essence, according to the master, while the latter is not. — س قده

The claim is not that all things are the intellect. As explained earlier, the intellect is all things: a separate, simple existence whose unity encompasses everything below it and gathers their actualities and perfections, but not their limits and deficiencies. This is “many within one,” not “one within many.” The higher levels contain all that is in the lower, and the lower is contained in the higher, in an ascending order. In this upward development, the soul does not cast off one form and put on another; it takes on one after another. Since a cause must be akin to its effect, and essences remain through the levels while existence is one reality whose distinguishing and shared features are the same, the higher level can contain the actualities of all lower beings in one simple way. This is possible only if the levels remain distinct; otherwise there would be no first effect followed by later effects, and many principles of philosophy would collapse. — س قده
That is, what comes later in the concept, not in reality; and its existence is dependent, not independent. — س قده
First, we do not accept that the First Effect’s unity is merely numerical. As noted earlier, it contains everything below it. — س قده

This objection applies to the master’s explicit wording, where the causal feature is taken in relation to the whole world, the Great Human, all existence, all good, and similar expressions. These suggest a unity made up of many things, so the author’s objection applies: a composite is more deserving of an essence than a simple thing. But it does not apply if the feature is understood as unrestricted existence, the all-embracing effusion, or another name for the sacred light. Unrestricted existence has no essence of its own; in one respect it is the existence of essences, and in another it is their real bringing into being. It is the manifestation of necessary existence, and there is no second manifestation beside it. — س قده

This claim has already been questioned. A caused existence is necessarily limited: something is affirmed of it and something denied. That limit is all we mean by an essence. Causation also always involves possibility, which is said to belong to an essence; every possible thing has a composite aspect of essence and existence. Intellects are simple identities only in relation to what is below them, not in relation to what is above. Absolute simplicity and pure being have no instance but God. So if an essence is denied of an intellect, it is denied only in relation to what is below it, since it is not limited relative to what is below it. — T. M. (editor).

“As existent” means without requiring bodily extension, dimensions, or multiplicity. In the opening notes on general principles, I explained that the unrestricted subject of metaphysics is unrestricted in just this sense. The reason is that natural and mathematical things depend on extension through space and time and on matter, while being as such does not. — س قده

At least two things would follow: existence, along with unity, individuation, and the like. Existence would come from one respect, while something other than existence would come from another. Thus existence would both come and not come from the respect that produces the other thing—a contradiction. — س قده

Their principle may be stated as: whenever a truly one being exists, two effects do not come from it. The author’s argument treats unity, thinghood, and similar features as one respect, not as several. It seems the word “nonexistence” may have been added by a copyist. The author’s point is that the rule depends on the possibility of a truly one being, which he thinks impossible. For him it is a true conditional with no instance. — س قده
The argument can be put this way: whenever two things come from a truly one being, it has contradictory features; and whenever it has contradictory features, it is composite. — س قده

People abandon general principles when a particular case seems to challenge them. Seeing no purpose in a thirsty person choosing one of two cups, they drop the principle that every voluntary act has a determining reason. Seeing that killing seems evil, they abandon the general truth that all existence is good. They should examine these cases instead of rejecting what is clear: evil is the absence of life, while all the steps leading to it are actual, good existences. The same approach applies to the first principle and to the rest. — س قده

That is, in the example of a human being and the structure of the mind: one might say this is also an external composition, since the general kind and defining feature in external compounds are treated as matter and form. — س قده
The phrase “and its being described as having parts that share common limits” should perhaps come before this. It may have been omitted by a copyist. — س قده
More consistently with the earlier wording, one should say: “its parts are aligned,” or “it is the shortest line joining two points,” and so on, as defining features of straightness. — س قده

The author generalizes “within” to include many defining parts and many attributes, as in a human being with many constituents and qualities such as knowledge, power, and will. “Not in existence or essence” means there is no multiplication in the whole, whether in existence or essence. “Not in the concrete” denies a plurality of matter and form; “not in the mind” denies a plurality of general kind and defining feature in external compounds; “not in thought” denies that same plurality in mental compounds such as accidents. None of these kinds of multiplicity applies to God, who has no essence, matter, form, broader kind, species, or added quality. — س قده

One might object that there is no problem: surely everyone who knows is also able, since nature does not give perceptive powers without also giving the motive powers on which ability depends. And how could someone able to act not also will, since an agent acts with awareness and will? The reply is that the claim concerns, for example, every knower through acquired knowledge being able to perform acquired crafts, or every knowing feature being the same as an ability, or every perceptive power being able to act. — س قده

This is a reply to the objection, and it contains two answers: the first is the discussion of bodily matter and its mode of existence; the second follows, beginning, “Or because each natural kind has another separate form…” — T. M. (editor).

The phrase “except that it knows it through its form” is a side note: the answer that follows is that it knows the matter through its ideal or intellectual form. Calling these forms “taken from” matter is loose. If the forms had the same presence and unity as their source, matter itself would possess that presence and unity. Rather, the forms descend from those higher forms, as the lower descends from the higher. — T. M. (editor).
Completing the argument by analogy shows that it is not a demonstration. In truth, this argument does not help. — T. M. (editor).

These are the qualities the author calls “knowledge that is not knowledge,” and so on. The related names are the well-known divine names that theology discusses: Living, Knowing, Willing, Powerful, Hearing, Seeing, and Speaking. — س قده

These are the attributes mentioned as “knowledge that is not knowledge,” “life like death,” and so forth: knowledge, life, will, power, hearing, sight, and speech. The Ashʿarites counted them as positive attributes, and many followed them. In truth, the basic attributes are three: knowledge, power, and life; hearing and sight follow from them. Will and speech, like other active attributes, reduce on analysis to real attributes and ultimately to the essential feature, as noted earlier. — T. M. (editor).
The earlier wording better suits the language of declaring God beyond all likeness. In this usage, however, “likeness” and “the source of sources” are invoked, though nothing resembles Him. — س قده

The argument depends on a special feature linking the effect to its cause. A careful commentator says that the earlier formulation better suits the language of declaring God beyond all likeness, while this one uses the words “likeness” and “similarity,” even though nothing resembles the first source. That criticism is right. The wording is awkward: it says that fit is likeness, and likeness is a kind of sameness in quality, ultimately a sameness in reality. If “likeness” and “sameness” are used in their technical senses, the argument would not apply to God or to any simple substantial cause, and the premise is itself disputed. If the words are used loosely, the added statements do no work; it would be enough to say that fit means sameness in reality. The further distinction—that sameness between two qualities is called likeness, while sameness between two subjects is called similarity—only makes the argument less clear. A better proof would say: a true cause must have an essential relation and a special bond to its effect, so that the effect’s existence depends on the cause’s existence. This bond requires a kind of shared nature between them, differing only in strength and weakness. If two things came from a truly simple One, either they would come from one aspect, making the One two, or from two aspects, making it composite. Both are impossible. — T. M. (editor).

The things that come together here are the knower and the known as descriptions. There is no relation between them, only a simple relation that does not repeat. The two sides of the relation that can be repeated by considering them separately are knowing and being known; these are mental, not external, distinctions. — T. M. (editor).
This is shown by the fact that reciprocal relations, without further qualification, form a separate class among the four kinds of opposition. — T. M. (editor).

A reciprocal relation means that each of two essences can be understood only by understanding the other, with the relation running both ways. This requires two distinct things in opposition: one and the same existence cannot belong to two distinct essences. The distinction can be drawn when the relation is between two real essences or between two conceptual ideas. — T. M. (editor).
That is, the thing itself, considered apart from incidental features surrounding it. — س قده

The point is that the very universal form that is part of the cause must, in a non-circular way, depend on matter, so that the two are necessarily linked and their combination gives rise to unity. “Form” here does not mean the universal concept or one of its scattered individuals. It means the natural universal—such as corporeality or a natural kind—which exists through its individuals, not separately. Yet the universal and its individual are considered in different ways, somewhat like a moving present and time. The form as unrestricted nature depends on matter in a general way; as a particular, bounded, shaped form, marked by division, connection, and other material features, it depends on matter specifically, since receptivity belongs to matter and particularization requires a basis. If this form were the first effect, it would itself need existence to cause anything below it, and its existence is that of its material individual, whose particularity depends on matter and its features. Then many things would come from the One. The author points to the need for motion and time because the form also depends on matter to persist: its individuals are maintained through succession, division, connection, and change, all of which belong to matter. — س قده

Some copies read “even if its existence in the creative realm comes before material things.” On that reading, its intellectual existence does not depend on matter, but the two are not necessarily linked, so it may not depend on matter at all. — س قده

The earlier point established the necessary link between form and matter. Now the author answers the opponent’s appeal to the claim that form is only a part of the cause: if form is in matter, many things would come from the One, as just shown. Its existence is also renewed in itself, so how could it be linked to the unchanging eternal source? And if matter is a partner in the cause, this can only mean that the true intellectual cause’s flow reaches form first and matter second. How, then, could this form be God’s first effect and also a source of what comes below it? — س قده

The opponent may be comparing the production of form from the source, taking “as they hold” with “so let it be possible for it to come forth.” Or the comparison may concern matter’s coming through form, taking “as they hold” with “through it.” On the latter reading, none of the author’s objections applies. — س قده
That is, the unrestricted celestial motion. By combining the particular motions of the spheres, the source produces particular matter and the distinct elemental forms. — س قده

This follows his view that the soul begins as bodily and survives as spiritual: in its first stage it is a natural principle, then moves through substantial change until it reaches an immaterial state with no quantity or quality. On that account, it is not prior in itself, much less in time. — س قده

The point is that every material power has a positional existence. The kind of production described must therefore be positional, since production depends on existence and position. But position cannot apply to what does not exist, or to matter itself, which has no position in its own right. — س قده

The outermost sphere, which determines directions, did not yet exist. This imagined sphere is contained within another; suppose it is in a high place, so change occurs in the containing sphere without a change in anything that contains it. — س قده

If a void were possible, there would be empty space around the contained sphere, to serve as the place of the containing sphere before it existed. That would require a void and would explain the greater by the lesser. — س قده

One could argue that the purely immaterial spirit is nobler than the spirit attached to a body; if the latter exists, the former should exist before it. Or one could say that natural kinds in our world exist, and are lower and less noble than their counterparts in the world of intellect, so they too should exist there first. — س قده
This issue was discussed earlier in the section on Platonic Forms in the discussion of essences. — T. M. (editor).

A firmer and shorter proof can be built on this premise: existence is fundamental and graded, differing in strength and weakness, actuality and potentiality, nobility and lowliness. Causation among possible beings, together with the claim that creation concerns existence itself, requires more than two levels of existence. One is necessarily God; the others are possible beings, some nobler than others. A caused existence is dependent and relational: it cannot stand by itself, but is grounded in an independent existence. Thus each essential level is dependent on the level above and supports the one below. In a three-level chain, the lowest is dependent on the middle, the middle independently supports the lowest but depends on the highest, and the highest independently supports all below it. If a lower, less noble level existed without a nobler level before it—whether the nobler level came at the same time, later, or never—then something that depends on a cause would exist without its cause, which is impossible. — T. M. (editor).
This applies to the First Effect. It does not rule out several effects from later intermediate causes, since they contain many aspects. — T. M. (editor).

Two further possibilities are that a simultaneous obstacle blocks the nobler being, or that a being of equal rank is an obstacle, even though God is admitted to be its cause. But both are ruled out because the principle is being applied only above the material world, where there is no opposition or obstruction. — T. M. (editor).

There are two reasons for this condition. First, the lower being must be of the same kind as the higher, as dim light is an imperfect form of strong light. White is not an imperfect form of light, nor is strong white the perfection of weak light; the same goes for intense and weak heat. Second, this makes it easier to establish that the nobler being is possible: if its essence is the same as the lower being’s, and the lower exists without contradiction, then the nobler one is plainly possible. That is less clear if their essences differ. — س قده

Existence is graded. In addition to the particular range belonging to each level, it has a range across the different levels. Essences drawn from these levels therefore differ in kind, while essences drawn from individual instances differ as individuals. One might object that many essences follow from many existences, while philosophers say many existences follow from many essences. The answer is that existence is the means by which essences multiply; the reverse claim is a way of proving the point. — س قده

The earlier proof applies only where the nobler being causes the lower one and no obstacle intervenes. This holds beyond the world of generation, but in that world nobler beings do not cause the lower ones, and events can coincide with obstacles. So the principle does not apply there. The wording is somewhat loose: the objection applies to perishable material things, but not to the heavenly bodies, which this tradition considers everlasting and beyond generation and decay. Yet the claim that the rule applies only to possible beings whose existence is stable excludes those bodies too, since their substance is in motion and their existence is not stable. — T. M. (editor).

This points to the principle’s application to the noble, necessary ends of things. In reality, these ends precede the things directed toward them, though they appear later. The author’s account therefore applies it to the First Intellect, the levels of the higher intellects, the universal intellects that govern natural kinds, the imaginal forms, the celestial bodies, and the noble ends that are necessary to existence. — T. M. (editor).
Dawānī calls the discussion difficult because of his own approach; on the author’s view, it is straightforward. — س قده

The two possibilities do not conflict, because a cause need only be possible in relation to its effect, not possible in itself. Nor do the two impossibilities conflict: a cause impossible in itself may still be possible in relation to its effect. The nobler level is impossible in itself, but it is possible in relation to the nobler possible being. It is impossible in itself, but not impossible in relation to that possible being. This is the distinction made by the inquirer and the skeptic. Since relational impossibility is broader than impossibility through another, it also covers their confusion between the two, as in Dawānī’s closing remark. — س قده
This is like two things impossible in themselves but with no relation between them: the impossibility of either does not rule out its possibility in relation to the other. — س قده

Up to “And we also say”: the point is not that the nobler possible has no existence for the objector, and so has no essence or possibility. That would invite two replies: unrealized possibilities such as the mythical ʿAnqāʾ still have possibility, at least in the mind; and it would create circularity, since recognizing the nobler possible’s essence and possibility would depend on knowing that it exists, while knowing it exists would depend on knowing its essence and possibility. Rather, possibilities depend on essences, essences depend on existences, and existences depend on necessary existence—or are its manifestation. Possibility means being able to receive existence or nonexistence from the Necessary Being, or from a possible being that depends on it. How, then, can the nobler being be possible if it would have to receive existence from a level that is impossible in itself? That is only ordinary imaginative speculation. It is like saying Zayd is possible because he could receive existence from a partner of God. — س قده

The author is not denying that a perfection can be impossible for God. He is denying that God lacks a perfection required by a real, existing possible being, as the objector alleges. The objector invents a possible essence that supposedly calls for a nobler feature in God, which God does not have; that is an absurd claim, especially since God is self-sufficient and the source of all needs. Every perfection we can imagine is in Him through necessary existence. As the saying goes, pure existence, than which nothing is more complete, cannot be given a second instance: whatever is imagined as another is that very same existence. — س قده
This excludes negative features, limits, and deficiencies from the argument. These are impossible for God and amount to negating a negation, which is affirmation. — س قده

If possibility, which is a kind of absence, were in God, He would be equally related to existence and nonexistence, which is impossible. If necessary existence were in Him as a feature, necessity through oneself and impossibility through another would coincide, also impossible. If impossibility in itself were in Him, the two kinds of impossibility would coincide, which was shown earlier to be impossible. The same reasoning applies to existence necessary through another. So existence and nonexistence are each either necessary in themselves or necessary through another. Only an essence can bear both an intrinsic and an extrinsic status: intrinsic possibility alongside necessity or impossibility through another. — T. M. (editor).
Especially since nobility and baseness are relative: each level is lower than what is above it and higher than what is below it. — س قده

There are no many separate individuals, finite or infinite, nor are they all gathered and ordered together. Rather, one immaterial being—the universal intellect—has, say, ten levels. It is also God’s knowledge, power, and greatest manifestation, indeed His fullest manifestation. A similar question and answer arise elsewhere in the author’s account of material development: he says there must be an intermediate stage between forms, such as vapor between water and air, algae between nonliving matter and plants, sponges between plants and animals, transformed creatures between animals and humans, an imaginal form between the command-spirit and the vaporous spirit, and balanced blood between the vaporous spirit and the natural body. One might ask whether this entails infinitely many intermediate stages, since each stage would require another between itself and either endpoint. The answer is that these levels form one continuous whole. The intermediate stages are not separated from the endpoints as the endpoints are separated from one another; all are one thing with levels. — س قده

In the downward order, the Principle of the Nobler Possible establishes it. The Principle of the Lower Possible then establishes that it has a soul, so its arrival at the rational destination—the governing intellect—does not involve a leap. Thus, on the upward path, a lower possible being, such as the imaginal form of a simple being, must precede the nobler possible being, the intellect. “Soul” here means the imaginal forms of simple beings; “plant power” means something like it, since plant powers properly belong to composites. “Animal life” and “imaginative power” refer to the next world, which is living and is itself knowledge and awareness. The First Teacher called these the plant word and animal word. The author aims to establish subtle truths within his own system, not familiar examples such as: if an animal has sight, it must also have the lower senses; if it has perception, it must also have the lower power of movement; if it has desire, it must also have the lower active power; and so on. — س قده
This is one of the familiar consequences of the principle. — س قده
Because its nature has no affinity with itself, being close to the world of divine command. — س قده

Matter individuates form, while form contributes as a partner in causing matter to exist. The two absences surrounding nature in motion are its prior potentiality and its later actuality. — T. M. (editor).

This is priority in essence, though also priority by nature. Form precedes matter as an incomplete cause, not as a complete cause and therefore not by full causal priority. Both are forms of priority by nature, but differ: potentiality precedes what is prepared for it as preparation precedes what it prepares, much like temporal priority, so the potential and its fulfillment cannot coincide. Form’s priority over matter differs because form is a co-agent and an incomplete cause of matter; matter can coexist with it, being before, with, and after it. Matter is called nonbeing because it is a thing’s potentiality, and potentiality as such is not yet a thing. — س قده

The explanation might more directly say that nature itself is accompanied by both absences, which are potentiality and matter. The author phrases it this way because potentiality and matter are the sources of past and future absence. — س قده

This explains why past and future absence do not taint the soul, as they do things that exist together. In the soul, this admixture concerns its acts, not its essence; in things that coexist, it concerns their very existence. — س قده
The soul is stable when considered through its successive stages of motion, but it is also shared in by those stages. — T. M. (editor).

This is different from the earlier analytic nonbeing, which meant that neither existence nor nonexistence is necessary to a thing’s essence. The author did not mention this type in that discussion, just as he did not mention the nonbeing tied to continuous extension, although nature is in motion; an attentive reader can infer the missing parts. The fourth kind—nonbeing required by spatial extension—applies specifically to quantitative form, which is receptive to dimensions in itself. — س قده

Aristotle called them the “three beginnings.” When some philosophers say nonbeing is a principle, they mean prior potentiality, without which a generated thing could not come to be as a generated thing. — س قده
That is, matter that exists before the form and bears its potentiality. — س قده

For example, the matter of a sperm: potentiality comes from it and is in it. A potentiality can belong to something, as the sperm’s body does; or it can be a potentiality for something, as the sperm’s specific form is. The thing being prepared, the capacity in it, and what gives it that capacity are distinct. The last determines what it is prepared to become; without it, the potentiality would not be directed toward a definite outcome. It varies by kind, and the potentiality varies accordingly: the human form prepares for humanity, the egg-form for a chick, and the seed-form for a plant. — س قده
That is, in actual existence. — س قده
Some of these arguments establish the First Intellect specifically, such as the third and fourth; the others establish an immaterial intellect in general. — T. M. (editor).

In the two reports, “light” means true light: intellect. Its spiritual nature is through the universal intellect, not an individual one. In Illuminationist language, the universal intellect is the overpowering light. All knowledge is light, since it is manifest in itself and makes other things—objects of knowledge—manifest. Intellect is knowing, knower, and known. Many transmitted reports support this idea. One report describes the higher world as forms without matter or potentiality, shining when God reveals Himself to them and radiating when they contemplate Him. Another, from Kumayl and ʿAlī, places intellect at the center of the individual and universal divine souls; this must mean the universal intellect. A further report from an Arab describes the universal divine soul as a divine power, a simple substance, alive in itself, whose origin is intellect, and then calls intellect a knowing substance that encompasses things, knows them before they exist, and is the cause of existing things and the end of all aims. This plainly supports the point. — س قده
This restates the argument given from the beginning of the chapter through the explanatory note. The author means to enumerate and complete the proofs. — س قده

As the wording suggests, “intellect” here means intellect in general—a broad category containing different kinds of intellect, each represented by one instance. The proof needs another unstated premise: that there are many intellects arranged in degrees of nobility. The next argument needs the same premise. — T. M. (editor).

“Kinds” refers to the earlier condition that the Principle of the Nobler Possible applies to higher and lower beings of the same specific kind. The author thinks it is enough that they share the same level or kind of existence. — س قده

The intellect “in potential” is a readiness, though it is already actual through its possession of first principles. It is called a capacity because it is what makes further readiness possible; as noted earlier, a readiness and what gives rise to it are inseparable. — س قده

Besides the difference in wording, one of these expressions suggests the light of the power itself, the other the light of the sun. In the comparison, the two lights stand for the intellect in act and the Active Intellect; the intellect’s own light is intuition and thought. — س قده

One might ask why forms alone are not enough, without the sacred substance serving as matter’s source. There are two reasons. First, the universal form is one in a general sense, while matter is numerically one; an efficient cause should be more unified than its effect, but here it would be less unified, unless form and matter were joint causes. Second, a body affects things through its position, but matter has no position by itself. Matter must therefore be caused by an intellect, which likewise has no position, rather than by an essence or form. This is not a claim that God could produce two changing things. It describes the actual order: essence is below both change and stability, and so this account reconciles the claims that natural kinds change and do not change. — س قده

One might object that an intellectual substance is stable, so a changing nature cannot come from it. The reply is that the intellect itself has an essence, and in that respect moves from nonexistence to existence, in a way like motion. It can therefore give rise to nature through its stable aspect, unlike God. — س قده

This is not circular. The philosophers’ division of possible beings into those that need only intrinsic possibility to receive existence and those that also need a preparatory possibility was made after they established the separate universal intellects. The argument here does not depend on those intellects being established first. “Completed kinds” means the natural kinds closest to us, considered as requiring an earlier, all-encompassing existence through the Giver’s generosity, not the essences of the intellects. This prior existence is different from the existence of natural kinds and universals themselves: though they too are created directly, they are at the lowest level of the eternal order, as the author says next. The proof can also be stated as follows: logical division requires two kinds of possible things—those whose intrinsic possibility is enough for existence and those that also need preparatory possibility. God is generous and gives without obstruction, granting each thing its due and bringing it to its proper level. This is how the author presents the twelfth proof later, when he divides things into four kinds. — س قده

One may object that there is no way to show this sufficiency before proving that separate beings exist. Merely imagining essences of this sort does not prove that such essences exist; until their existence is established, they are only concepts, and their essences are tied to those existences. — T. M. (editor).
One may also ask why some kinds could not depend on beings that do not exist always or for the most part, as suggested by kinds that have died out. — T. M. (editor).

This points to another meaning: the differences between natural kinds in this world depend on differences among the higher kinds of intellects. These are the active aspects and levels of God’s power and knowledge; the differences cannot come directly from the One because of His unity and simplicity. — س قده

Although the tenth proof resembles the fifth, they differ. The fifth concerns the rational soul and proceeds through motion, its gradual passage from potentiality to actuality; this one concerns the celestial sphere and proceeds through change in general. The second version of the tenth proof differs from the eighth: the latter concerns the ends of natural kinds, directed toward the universal intellects that govern them; this one concerns the ends of the spheres, directed toward the nine higher intellects. The eighth follows the Illuminationist path; this one follows the approach of Aristotle’s followers, or the approach shared by both. — س قده
Especially since, in itself, the higher realm is the world of divine command, set against the world of creation, as in the verse, “His are creation and command.” — س قده
These forms are immaterial, and philosophers infer from their immateriality that rational souls are immaterial. How much more, then, should their true counterparts in reality be immaterial? — س قده

These forms are universal intellectual forms, separate from matter and its features. If they existed only in rational souls or in the Active Intellect, they would depend on and inhere in something else, and would not be intellects themselves. If they exist in themselves, they are universal intellects and luminous forms, as Plato, Socrates, and their followers held: when the intellect grasps universals, it receives them from these forms. — س قده

There is a difficulty here. If the Active Intellect contains acquired knowledge, the truth of that knowledge depends on other things in the world that match it. Then those external instances, not the Active Intellect’s knowledge, are what our true ideas really match, and the claim that our ideas match the Active Intellect’s knowledge does no work. If its knowledge is direct or present knowledge, two problems arise: first, it would consist of actual existences that our ideas match whether or not an intellect knew them, so the intellect would not need to exist; second, some truths concern subjects that do not exist, as in “the absence of a cause causes the absence of its effect,” and such things cannot be known through direct presence. A possible reply, drawn from the earlier discussion of why a possible thing’s nonexistence needs a cause, is that the mind first finds existence predicated of itself, then necessarily extends it to the essence drawn from it, and finally to conceptual notions drawn from that essence. Judgments formed in this way can be true without having a match either in the mind or outside it; their match lies in the wider field of what is established, including existence, essence, and conceptual notions. Universal truths of this kind correspond to forms of direct knowledge in the intellectual world. — T. M. (editor).
This is the basis for the author’s twelfth argument. — س قده

That is, in the phrase “the identity flowed from it,” to avoid implying that essence is created. “Identity” could mean essence in the phrase “because it had no identity,” but using it for existence in both places keeps the wording consistent. — س قده

This means the level where all things are absorbed into God, with no separate “you” or “I”; no one can grasp this state in ordinary language. At the level where individual things exist, each is truly present with God, since it cannot be separated from Him. — س قده

The comparison concerns the Active Intellect and the human intellect. On the illumination account, the Active Intellect’s light shines on the knowing soul as the sun shines on sight. When the two lights meet, the soul sees the universal forms in the Active Intellect themselves; it does not receive new imprints. This resembles the view that rays leave the eye and reflect from a mirror to the object itself. On the “overflow” account, the forms are imprinted in the soul as well. The author’s own view, as indicated earlier, is neither: the soul and the Active Intellect become one, as the soul is absorbed into it. — س قده
The difficulty concerns lapses of attention and forgetting. The wording hints at this distinction. — س قده

The proposed distinction works for sensory images, but not for intelligible ideas. It assumes that the Active Intellect is a storehouse for the knowing intellect; then false universal ideas must also be there, since we can both lose sight of and forget them. — س قده
Perhaps there was not enough time to give a full answer or reveal certain points, as the author will do in his own solution. The great al-Muḥaqqiq Tusi was not incapable of answering. — س قده

The reply seems to say that the parts of a false judgment—its subject, predicate, and relation—have counterparts in the Active Intellect, but not the judgment’s affirmation, which is an act of estimation. Yet this would mean that neither true nor false universal affirmations need an intellectual counterpart as affirmations. There is no reason to grant a match only to true affirmations. The argument would then rely only on the conceptual parts and their being remembered or forgotten, which raises two problems: the conclusion would be narrower than the claim it is meant to prove, while the proof itself would apply more broadly than that conclusion. — T. M. (editor).

If the Active Intellect does not affirm the relation, then it does not judge it. If knowledge means affirming a relation, the Active Intellect would only conceive the terms, not know the proposition. But universal judgments, true or false, are themselves universal. Just as universal concepts are stored in the Active Intellect, so are universal affirmations, including false ones: we can lose sight of and forget false universal judgments. The distinction between momentary inattention and forgetting cannot be drawn without appealing again to the Active Intellect, so the problem remains. A false judgment represented there without assent is a judgment in the primary sense of the term, but not in the ordinary sense. — س قده

The wording suggests that Dawānī denied universal relations altogether. In fact, he denied only the special, necessary joining found in false judgments. He explicitly says that the Active Intellect preserves and affirms true judgments. The author’s point is that Dawānī must deny that special joining too: necessary assent to false judgments, and the certainty of someone who is confidently mistaken, also come from the Active Intellect, since it is a unified, universal, immaterial existence. This objection hints at the more precise account the author is about to give. — س قده
